common_name: Mexican Giant Echeveria (Oversized Blue-Grey Rosette Hens-and-Chicks)

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring and set into fast-draining, mineral succulent mix in full sun; this selection builds an unusually large rosette compared to typical colorata.

directions: Mexican Giant is a selected clone of Echeveria colorata prized for building a notably larger, chalky blue-grey rosette than typical seed-grown plants, with thick, pointed leaves that pick up pink-red tips under bright light and cool temperatures. It produces coral-pink, bell-shaped flowers on arching stalks in late winter to spring. Grow in gritty, mineral soil with excellent drainage and full sun, watering only when the soil has dried completely. Protect from prolonged freezing and wet winter soil, both of which cause rot far faster than cold alone.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring in gritty mix and grow on in full sun; Frosty carries a dense coat of fine white hairs over its leaves and stems.

directions: Frosty is a fuzzy-leaved selection of the plush plant, Echeveria pulvinata, coated in short white hairs that give the pale green, paddle-shaped leaves a silvery sheen and soften red winter blushing seen on the species. Branching stems become semi-shrubby with age, and red-orange tubular flowers appear in winter and early spring. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and avoid overhead watering, since trapped moisture in the fuzzy leaf surface promotes rot and spotting. Light winter chill intensifies foliage color without the deeper red tones of unselected plants.

planting.note: Detach loose rolling offsets in spring or summer and press lightly onto gritty, well-drained soil; they root quickly without being buried.

directions: Preissii is an old alpine-garden selection of Jovibarba hirta valued for its tight, globular, pale green rosettes fringed with fine cilia along the leaf margins, smaller and more uniform than typical seed-grown hirta. True to the genus, loose chicks detach freely and roll away from the mother rosette to self-sow new colonies across gravelly ground. Grow in lean, mineral soil in full sun, where compact growth and good color hold best; richer soil or shade causes rosettes to loosen and stretch. It is fully winter hardy and needs no protection beyond sharp drainage.

common_name: Thunderhead Japanese Black Pine (Dense Dwarf Candle-Tip Pine)

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; bright white winter buds make this cultivar easy to identify and site as a specimen.

directions: Thunderhead is a dwarf Japanese black pine selection prized for extremely dense, dark green needles crowded onto short, stout shoots, with conspicuous bright white candles of new growth emerging each spring in striking contrast to the foliage. Its naturally compact, irregular mounding habit suits rock gardens, large containers, and bonsai training without the heavy pruning typical species pines require. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, and candle-prune in late spring only if an even tighter, more formal outline is wanted. It tolerates salt spray and wind, making it a reliable choice in coastal plantings.

common_name: Schoodic Jack Pine (Prostrate Coastal Dwarf Pine)

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring; this prostrate selection spreads wide and low rather than gaining height, so give it ample horizontal room.

directions: Schoodic is a prostrate, ground-hugging selection of jack pine selected by Al Fordham of the Arnold Arboretum from seed collected on Schoodic Point in Acadia National Park, Maine, where constant wind exposure naturally flattens the species' growth. Plants retain this low, spreading habit under cultivation, forming a dense mat of short, twisted, dark green needles well below typical jack pine height. It thrives in poor, sandy, acidic soil and full sun, tolerating wind, salt spray, and drought once established. Use it to cover slopes or rock garden edges where an exceptionally tough, low conifer is needed.

planting.note: Transplant in spring into moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, where foliage color holds best without scorching.

directions: Everitt's Golden is a slow-growing dwarf Canadian hemlock selection whose new spring growth emerges bright golden-yellow before settling to a yellow-green that persists better through summer than most golden conifers. Its dense, irregular, broadly conical habit stays compact for many years without pruning. Plant in cool, moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and give it partial shade in hot climates, since full, intense afternoon sun can scorch the gold foliage. Protect roots with mulch and avoid hot, dry sites, as hemlocks are shallow-rooted and sensitive to drought stress and woolly adelgid in affected regions.

common_name: Peve Tijn Serbian Spruce (Compact Dwarf Dutch Golden Selection)

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; this slow Dutch selection, a golden sport found on P. omorika 'Nana' by Piet Vergeldt, keeps a tidy narrow-conical outline with minimal care.

directions: Peve Tijn is a dwarf Serbian spruce introduced by Dutch conifer grower Piet Vergeldt as a golden-foliage sport of 'Nana', selected for a dense, narrowly conical habit considerably slower and smaller than the species. It keeps good symmetry without shearing, making it useful as a small accent or foundation specimen where a full-size Serbian spruce would outgrow the space. Grow in well-drained soil in full sun; Serbian spruce tolerates alkaline soil, air pollution, and heat better than most spruces. Little pruning is required beyond removing the occasional competing leader.

common_name: Waldbrunn Dwarf Colorado Spruce (Compact Blue German Selection)

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring into well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest blue needle color; selected by Rolf Friedrich of Waldbrunn, Germany in 1984.

directions: Waldbrunn is a German-origin dwarf selection of Colorado blue spruce forming a dense, flattened-globose bush well below the height of seed-grown trees, with stiff, sharply pointed needles in a clear silvery blue. Its compact habit and slow growth rate make it practical for smaller gardens where standard Colorado spruce would quickly overwhelm the space. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; this spruce tolerates heat, cold, and some drought once established but performs poorly in wet, poorly drained ground. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead interior wood.

common_name: Hillside Creeper Scots Pine (Low Spreading Groundcover Pine)

planting.note: Transplant grafted or layered stock in spring; give it wide lateral room since it spreads far faster than it climbs. Selected by Layne Ziegenfuss of Hillside Nursery, Lehighton, PA.

directions: Hillside Creeper is a prostrate selection of Scots pine that stays only a foot or so tall while spreading several feet wide, its branches hugging the contours of the ground or draping over walls and boulders. Blue-green needles and a loose, informal texture distinguish it from the stiffer habit of typical dwarf pine cultivars. Grow in full sun in well-drained, even sandy or rocky soil, where it tolerates drought and poor fertility once established. Use it on slopes, large rock gardens, or trained over a low wall where its spreading habit can be shown off.

common_name: Glauca Compacta Subalpine Fir (Dwarf Blue Corkbark Fir)

planting.note: Transplant grafted stock in spring into cool, well-drained soil in full sun; give it good air circulation and avoid hot, humid sites.

directions: Glauca Compacta is a dwarf, slow-growing selection of subalpine fir with dense, narrowly conical form and short, powder-blue needles considerably more compact than the corky-barked species trees found in high western mountains. It keeps a neat, symmetrical outline for many years without pruning, making it a dependable small specimen conifer. Grow in cool, moist, well-drained soil in full sun, and site it where summer heat and humidity are moderate, since this high-elevation species struggles in hot, humid climates. Good air movement around the crown helps prevent fungal needle problems.
